classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied substitution-and-comparison test to exponential, cube-root, rational and radical functions, then confirm the corresponding symmetry in software plots. The hardest decisions are handling the real cube-root sign and recognising symmetric restricted domains; the method is supplied throughout.

content.prompt: [Algebra and Technology] Odd and even functions can also be non-polynomial. In each case following, simplify $f(-x)$ and compare with $f(x)$ and $-f(x)$ to determine whether it is odd or even. Then confirm your answer by plotting the function on appropriate graphing software.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\frac{2^{-x}+2^{-(-x)}}{2}\\f(-x)&=\frac{2^{-x}+2^x}{2}\\f(-x)&=f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore $f$ is even. A software plot confirms reflection symmetry in the $y$-axis, with minimum $(0,1)$.

spec.description: Even exponential sum with minimum at (0,1).
spec.answerVisibility: Answer graph representing the expected software plot.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\frac{2^{-x}-2^{-(-x)}}{2}\\f(-x)&=\frac{2^{-x}-2^x}{2}\\f(-x)&=-\frac{2^x-2^{-x}}{2}\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore $f$ is odd. A software plot confirms $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the origin.

spec.description: Increasing odd exponential difference through the origin.
spec.answerVisibility: Answer graph representing the expected software plot.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\sqrt[3]{-x}\\f(-x)&=-\sqrt[3]{x}\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore $f$ is odd. A software plot through $(-1,-1)$, $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ confirms origin symmetry.

spec.description: Cube-root graph with dashed guides to (±1,±1).
spec.mathematics: Parameterisation (t³,t) gives the real cube-root graph.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\left(\sqrt[3]{-x}\right)^2\\f(-x)&=\left(-\sqrt[3]{x}\right)^2\\f(-x)&=\left(\sqrt[3]{x}\right)^2\\f(-x)&=f(x)\end{align*}$$
Therefore $f$ is even. A software plot has a cusp at the origin and reflection symmetry in the $y$-axis.

spec.description: Even squared-cube-root graph through (±1,1), with cusp at the origin.
spec.mathematics: Parameterisation (t³,t²) preserves the cusp and real domain.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\frac{-x}{(-x)^2-4}\\f(-x)&=-\frac{x}{x^2-4}\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain excludes $x=\pm2$ and is symmetric about $0$. Therefore $f$ is odd. A software plot confirms origin symmetry, vertical asymptotes $x=\pm2$ and horizontal asymptote $y=0$.

spec.description: Odd rational graph with three branches and dashed vertical asymptotes at ±2.
spec.mathematics: y=x/(x²−4), x≠±2. The x-axis is the horizontal asymptote.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\frac{2}{(-x)^2-4}\\f(-x)&=\frac{2}{x^2-4}\\f(-x)&=f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain excludes $x=\pm2$ and is symmetric about $0$. Therefore $f$ is even. A software plot confirms $y$-axis symmetry, vertical asymptotes $x=\pm2$, horizontal asymptote $y=0$ and $y$-intercept $-\tfrac12$.

spec.description: Even rational graph with positive outer branches and negative central branch.
spec.mathematics: y=2/(x²−4), x≠±2. Vertical asymptotes ±2, horizontal asymptote y=0, y-intercept -1/2.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=\sqrt{9-(-x)^2}\\f(-x)&=\sqrt{9-x^2}\\f(-x)&=f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain is $-3\le x\le3$, symmetric about $0$. Therefore $f$ is even. A software plot gives the upper semicircle of radius $3$, confirming $y$-axis symmetry.

spec.description: Upper semicircle with closed endpoints at ±3 and maximum (0,3).
spec.mathematics: x²+y²=9 with y≥0. Equal axis units preserve the circle.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=(-x)\sqrt{9-(-x)^2}\\f(-x)&=-x\sqrt{9-x^2}\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain is $-3\le x\le3$, symmetric about $0$. Therefore $f$ is odd. A software plot has zeroes at $-3,0,3$, a negative left lobe and a positive right lobe, confirming origin symmetry.

spec.description: Bounded odd curve with closed endpoints at (-3,0),(3,0), negative left lobe and positive right lobe.
spec.mathematics: y=x√(9−x²), -3≤x≤3. Parameterisation x=3 sin(t), y=9 sin(t)cos(t), -90°≤t≤90°.
